19687-the-square-of-sevens-an-authoritat:
Cartomancy is fortune-telling with ordinary playing cards. The Square of Sevens, issued in 1896, presents itself as an authoritative method of that art. Its editor praises the source text's solemn faith in its own mysteries. The old spellings and capital letters mark it as an early eighteenth-century work. Quaint phrases sit beside strict attention to business.

Books of this sort taught readers to lay cards in set patterns. Each position and card carried a fixed meaning. The square of sevens gives the method its shape. Beyond belief or doubt, the book has real literary flavor. It preserves how fortune-tellers once spoke to clients. Historians of popular magic still cite such manuals.
19830-moody-s-anecdotes-and-illustration:
Dwight L. Moody, the great revival preacher, filled sermons with stories. Moody's Anecdotes and Illustrations collects them from his revival work. The compiler kept Moody's own idiom strictly, he promises. Gold, he says, is scattered through the volume. The pieces come from Chicago tabernacle meetings and New York's Hippodrome services. Daily press reports supplied much of the text.

Moody's anecdotes were tools, not ornaments. Each short story aimed a doctrine at a hearer's conscience. Preachers mined collections like this for their own sermons. The book preserves revival preaching at its most practical. Moody's plain talk reached millions in his lifetime. These pages show the workshop behind the sermons.
20065-twenty-years-of-congress-volume-2-:
James G. Blaine wrote Twenty Years of Congress, and volume two runs from Lincoln to Garfield. It also reviews the events that led to the change of 1860. Blaine served in Congress through much of that span himself. Few men knew its fights and leaders from so close at hand.

The volume records Lincoln's death on April 15, 1865, in plain detail. Three hours later, Andrew Johnson took the oath as president. Chief Justice Chase gave that oath while the cabinet looked on. Readers get war, loss, and rebuilding told by a man who sat in the room.
20586-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-3-christ:
In the Yule-Log Glow, Book 3 gathers Christmas poems from round the world, published in 1891 as part of a set for holiday reading. The poems come from many lands and ages, all turned toward the season. Some are carols, and some are literary verses on the holy night.

One piece borrows Shakespeare's famous lines on the season. Some say that ever against the time when our Saviour's birth is celebrated, the bird of dawning sings all night long. Then no spirit dares stir abroad, and the nights are wholesome. The set was made for family reading by firelight.
21271-chocolate-or-an-indian-drinke-by-t:
Antonio Colmenero of Ledesma, a Spanish doctor, wrote this tract on chocolate. Captain James Wadsworth translated it into English for a London edition of 1652. Its title promises that wise and moderate use of the Indian drink preserves health and cures sickness, above all the plague of the guts. Beauty and easier childbirth are also claimed.

Wadsworth says the tract and the chocolate itself were first admitted to the English court under Lord Conway's patronage. The book explains the name, from Mexican words for water and the noise of stirring. It stands among the first English works promoting a drink that would reshape European habits.
21822-a-lecture-on-heads-as-delivered-by:
Heads, forty-seven of them in pictures, supply the jokes in George Alexander Stevens's famous Lecture on Heads, a one-man stage show of the 1700s. Stevens toured it through London and nearly every large town in England and Ireland to huge success. Fellow wits like Churchill and Shuter fed him new hints along the way. Later performers, Charles Lee Lewes among them, kept delivering it with additions by Mr. Pilon.

The act mocked the types of the age through carved and pictured heads, with an essay on satire added at the end. This 1812 edition answers a swarm of pirated copies that had mangled the act. It preserves a landmark of solo stage comedy, part script, part picture book.
22110-martian-v-f-w:
G. L. Vandenburg's Martian V. F. W. is a short science fiction story with a grim joke in its title. The initials twist the Veterans of Foreign Wars into veterans of a future war on Mars. His character Cruthers faces the Martians at close range. They are ants six feet tall, coloured yellow, brown, and a third bright hue, with goggle eyes that roll when they speak.

Vandenburg plays the meeting for wonder and unease at once. Earthmen who thought themselves conquerors meet beings built to unsettle them. The story appeared in the pulp magazines that fed young science fiction fans. Its brief length and sharp image are typical of that fast, idea-driven market.

journals-of-two-expeditions-into-the-int:
John Oxley's Journals of Two Expeditions into the Interior of New South Wales record government surveys of 1817 and 1818. Oxley was surveyor general of the territory and a lieutenant of the Royal Navy. The book appeared with maps and views of the newly discovered country. Appendices print his instructions, official reports, and letters to the governor.

One appendix gives Mr. Evans's diary for part of July 1818. Others report Oxley's return and his discovery of Port Stephens. Tables of population, land under cultivation, and stock for 1813 to 1817 close the volume. The journals show exploration as official work: orders, surveys, and reports. They remain basic sources for the first opening of inland New South Wales.
journals-of-two-expeditions-of-discovery:
Volume one of George Grey's Journals of Two Expeditions of Discovery covers his travels in north-west and western Australia. The expeditions ran through 1837, 1838, and 1839, under the authority of the British government. Grey later became governor of South Australia. The London edition of 1841 fills two volumes, of which this is the first.

The title page promises many newly discovered, fertile districts described in detail. It also promises observations on the moral and physical condition of the Aboriginal inhabitants. Grey wrote as both explorer and official, judging land for settlement as he crossed it. His journals became standard reading on western Australia's coasts and peoples. This volume opens that record with the first of the two expeditions.
maxims-and-opinions-of-field-marshal-his:
George Henry Francis edited the Maxims and Opinions of the Duke of Wellington. Henry Colburn printed the book in London in 1845. It draws on Wellington's writings and speeches across more than fifty years.

A short life of the duke stands at the front of the book. The editor says most past works stress the duke's wars alone. His years as a minister and statesman, he argues, got far less care. These pages let readers judge Wellington's claims in that second, civic life. The duke's own words, not tales about him, fill most pages. Readers can weigh his views on war, rule, and public duty.
